newsitem.title: USA: U.S. poultry producers oppose EU standards.
newsitem.headline: U.S. poultry producers oppose EU standards.

text.p: U.S. poultry producers said Tuesday they were unwilling to back away from improvements in food safety standards in order to meet the demands of European trade negotiators for inspection system equivalency.
U.S. and European Union negotiators were to resume talks on Tuesday afternoon on meat and poultry inspection standards.

The Europeans want the United States to adopt the EU's rules that are "lacking in commitment to overall microbiological quality and wholesomeness," said Kenneth May, technical advisor to the National Broiler Council.

May said U.S. poultry production has grown rapidly in the past 20 years -- from average U.S. consumption of 52 pounds per person in 1977 to 93 pounds per person in 1997 -- because of consumer confidence in the quality of poultry products.

"The European Union officials want us to go back to where we stood 20 years ago and ignore all the scientific findings and technological advancements that have been made in that time," May said in a statement.

Alice Hurlburg, director of scientific affairs for the National Turkey Federation, said U.S. poultry and meat plants are adopting a sophisticated process control method known as Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points while the EU has nothing like HACCP in place.

The EU also objects to the U.S. use of water with a small amount of chlorine in it when processing poultry and red meat. Similar anti-bacterial procedures are used in Britain, a member of the EU, she said.

"Some British processing plants use chlorine at higher levels than we do," Hurlburg said. "While U.S. plants use 20 to 50 parts per million (ppm), concentrations between 70 and 100 ppm were being used in some plants in the UK in 1996."
